content.question: In the demo the instructor creates a Kotlin file from the project view. Which menu sequence in Android Studio produces a new Kotlin file (not class) in the appropriate package?

options.text: Right‑click package → New → Kotlin Class/File → choose 'File' and enter name
File → New → Java Class → change extension to .kt manually
Right‑click res/layout → New → Kotlin File
Tools → Kotlin → New Kotlin File

content.explanation: The instructor right‑clicked the package (com.myandroid...) → New → Kotlin class/file, selected 'File' and provided the file name (e.g., MainKTFile).
hints: Create files from the package node
Use New → Kotlin class/file and choose 'File'

content.question: What is the role of the 'main' function in a standalone Kotlin file demonstrated in the video?

options.text: It is the entry point where Kotlin starts executing the file's code
It defines a UI layout for the activity
It registers the activity in AndroidManifest.xml
It automatically runs on app launch without configuration

content.explanation: The 'main' function is the starting point for running the Kotlin file and without it the file is not runnable by the IDE's run action.
hints: Kotlin needs a starting function to run a file
Removing main makes the file unrunnable

content.question: When the instructor runs the Kotlin file, a small play button appears next to the code. What does selecting that run action do compared with using the top 'app' run configuration?

options.text: Runs only the selected Kotlin file (its main), not the whole Android app
Builds and deploys the entire Android app to the emulator
Opens a debug console connected to the device
Converts the Kotlin file to Java and runs it

content.explanation: The inline run action executes the single Kotlin file (its main function), whereas the top app configuration builds and runs the Android application package.
hints: Look at the run target label (mainKTFile vs app)
Inline run is useful for quick scripts or tests

content.question: Which Kotlin function call does the instructor use to print a line of text and then move to the next line in the run window?

options.text: println("text")
print("text")
System.out.print("text")
Log.d("TAG", "text")

content.explanation: The instructor uses println which prints the text and advances to the next line; print does not add a newline.
hints: println vs print
Check differences in output layout

content.question: What observable difference did the instructor demonstrate between 'print' and 'println' when multiple calls are made?

options.text: 'println' prints each call on a new line; 'print' continues on the same line
'print' prints with extra spacing; 'println' removes spacing
'print' is slower than 'println'
They behave identically in Kotlin

content.explanation: 'println' appends a newline after printing; 'print' does not, so subsequent output appears on the same line.
hints: Try two prints vs two printlns
Observe run output lines

content.question: The instructor prints different kinds of literals: text, integers, decimals and booleans. In Kotlin, which of the following is a valid decimal literal the instructor used in the demo?
content.explanation: Decimal numbers in Kotlin use a dot (.) as the decimal separator, e.g., 12.1234 was shown in the demo.
hints: Use '.' for decimals
Not a string unless quoted

content.question: When introducing variables the instructor explained 'val' vs 'var'. Which statement correctly describes the difference?

options.text: 'val' defines an immutable value (cannot be reassigned); 'var' defines a mutable variable (can be reassigned)
'val' creates a global variable; 'var' creates a local variable
'val' is for integer only; 'var' is for strings only
'val' and 'var' are interchangeable

content.explanation: 'val' creates a read‑only reference (like a final variable), while 'var' allows reassignment.
hints: Try reassigning a 'val' to see the IDE error
Use 'var' when you need to change the value

content.question: The instructor showed that after declaring a 'val' without assignment the IDE complained. What must you provide when declaring a 'val' in that context?

options.text: An initial value or an explicit type with later initialization (e.g., val x: Int = 3)
A visibility modifier like 'private'
A lateinit keyword
A semicolon at the end of the line

content.explanation: A 'val' must be initialized where declared (or declared with a type and later set in constructor), otherwise the IDE shows an error; 'lateinit' is allowed only for var with non-null types.
hints: val requires initialization
'lateinit' cannot be used with val

content.question: In the demo the instructor prints a variable's value using println after declaring it. Which sequence is required to correctly print the stored value?

options.text: Declare the variable (val/var), assign a value, then call println(variableName)
Call println before declaring the variable
Declare the variable without assignment and println will auto-print null
Use println("$variableName") without declaring variable

content.explanation: You must declare and assign the variable before using it; println(variableName) prints the current value.
hints: Initialize variables before use
Kotlin is statically typed and checks usages

content.question: Which of the following is a best practice the instructor suggested to avoid repeatedly typing the same literal (like 'Hello Android') throughout a file?

options.text: Store the literal in a variable and reuse the variable where needed
Copy and paste the literal everywhere
Write the literal inside comments and refer to it
Always hardcode the literal to keep code explicit

content.explanation: Defining a variable reduces duplication and makes updates easier, as demonstrated when the instructor replaced repeated text with a variable reference.
hints: Use val for constants you won't change
Use var if the value must be updated

content.question: The instructor changed a variable declared with 'var' to a new value later in the code. Which behaviour will you see when you run the program after reassigning the variable?

options.text: The later assigned value is printed (variable holds the new value)
The original value is retained and printed
The program will crash at runtime
Kotlin silently ignores reassignment

content.explanation: A 'var' can be reassigned; subsequent reads return the newest value as shown in the demo where the variable printed the updated string.
hints: Use var to allow value changes
Observe output after reassignment

content.question: What will happen to the run/play icon and the ability to run the file if you rename or remove the 'main' function in a Kotlin script as shown in the episode?

options.text: The play icon disappears and the file becomes non-runnable because there is no entry point
The file will still run using the previous configuration
Android Studio will auto-create a default main function
The file will run as an Android activity instead

content.explanation: Without a valid main function the inline run action is removed and Kotlin cannot run the file; the instructor showed the cross mark indicating the file is no longer runnable.
hints: Kotlin needs an entry point to run a file
Restoring main brings run icon back
